articleTitle: Stability Margins and Error Amplification in Asymmetric Bidirectional Platoon Control
publicationTitle: 2025 SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (SICE ISCS)
abstract: Vehicle platooning has attracted substantial attention as an approach to improve transportation network efficiency and promote vehicle autonomy. Nevertheless, it is widely recognized that increasing the platoon length can lead to various problems, including string instability. This study addresses the challenge of coordinating a line of vehicles travelling along a single dimension to ensure they maintain a constant spacing while following a lead vehicle. We examine an asymmetric bidirectional control strategy, where the control action depends unevenly between the adjacent vehicles governed by an adjustable weight factor. Our findings reveal that the choice of this weight factor involves a trade-off between the convergence rate of spacing errors and the suppression of error amplification along the string. While asymmetric control can stabilize errors near the leader or enhance convergence rates in small or medium-sized platoons, it risks amplifying errors in large-scale systems. The symmetric configuration consistently provides robust performance, minimizing sensitivity to high-frequency disturbances and ensuring bounded <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$H_{\infty}$</tex> -norms across varying platoon lengths and system dynamics.

articleTitle: Dimension of Lift and Numerical Stability in Extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition
publicationTitle: 2025 SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (SICE ISCS)
abstract: Extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition (EDMD), a data-driven modeling method, has gained interest because the method can construct an accurate linear model using the lifting function. The dimension of the lift is known to be related to the accuracy of the linear model. Several studies have shown that the high dimension of the lift can contribute to the modeling accuracy. However, the appropriate dimension of the lift needs to be clarified because the previous results have dealt with limited dimensions. This research defines the higher dimension of the lift than previous studies and discusses the relationships between the dimension of the lift and numerical stability using the condition number. In numerical simulations, the results reveal that the high dimension of the lift is one of the reasons that promotes numerical instability. Our study gives new indicators when the dimension of the lift is defined.

articleTitle: Enhancement of Beam Switching in Single Element Antenna Using Machine Learning
publicationTitle: 2025 SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (SICE ISCS)
abstract: This paper presents the design of a single circular microstrip antenna that operates at a frequency of 2.6 GHz, which is one of the frequencies used in 5G wireless communications. The antenna is capable of beam switching in eight directions and incorporates machine learning techniques into its design. This integration aids in predicting the main beam direction and the return loss. The input parameters include the distance between short circuit points, the number of short circuit holes, the short circuit direction, and the radius from the center to the position of the short-circuit holes. The output parameters consist of the main beam direction and the return loss, which are essential for the antenna's beam switching functionality. A total of 140 data sets were collected from the antenna designs in the CST Studio Suite, which were used to predict the main beam direction and the return loss. Four machine learning algorithms were applied for prediction: Gradient Regression, Lasso Regression, Linear Regression, and Random Forest. The results from these four algorithms were compared to determine which provided the best outcomes for predicting the main beam direction and the return loss. Among all the algorithms tested, the Random Forest algorithm yielded the best results.

Index Terms: Least Absolute Shrinkage And Selection Operator

articleTitle: Experimental Validation of Multi-UAV Applications: Formation Flight and Decentralized Target Estimation
publicationTitle: 2025 SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (SICE ISCS)
abstract: This paper describes the experimental validation of two multi-UAV applications in an indoor environment. In particular, a formation flight task and a decentralized estimation procedure are analyzed for quad-copter platforms. First, the experimental setup is discussed, focusing on the hardware chosen for the navigation, control, and guidance layers of the UAVs. For the first application, a flocking protocol previously designed by the authors is implemented, proving satisfactory performance in terms of inter-agent distance and transient behavior. For the second application, a decentralized Kalman Filter is employed to collaboratively estimate the position of an ArUco marker. The experimental results show a successful information fusion by sharing the UAVs' measurements performed by onboard cameras.

articleTitle: Model-Free Predictive Control in Anaerobic Digestion Wastewater Treatment
publicationTitle: 2025 SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (SICE ISCS)
abstract: Anaerobic digestion is a wastewater treatment method that utilizes bacterial decomposition to convert organic matter into biogas, which provides both environmental and economic benefits. However, controlling biogas production in anaerobic digestion systems poses significant challenges due to the complexity and non-linearity of the digestion process. This study explores the application of model-free predictive control for anaerobic digestion systems, utilizing only inputoutput data without using mathematical models as in conventional control approaches. Previous research has demonstrated the applicability of this approach for nonlinear systems, particularly in multi-input, multi-output nonlinear systems. In this study extends the methodology to controlling in methane production of anaerobic digestion systems, evaluating its effectiveness through numerical simulations.

articleTitle: Consensus Control for Resilient Multi-Agent Systems Considering Leader Failure
publicationTitle: 2025 SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (SICE ISCS)
abstract: In this paper, we study a consensus control problem for resilient multi-agent systems considering leader failure. We present cooperative control to solve the formation problem, enabling the agents to maintain relative positions even if any agent, including the leader, malfunctions. To accomplish this goal, we designed an algorithm that implements distributed observers for fault detection to assess each agent's reliability. The algorithm reduces the effect of faults by limiting information exchange with low-reliability agents. Next, we extended the adjacency matrix so that any follower can replace the leader in response to the leader's failure. Finally, we verify the proposed method through simulations.

articleTitle: Enhancing Non-Cooperative Rendezvous Through Differential Drag Estimation Using Disturbance Observer
publicationTitle: 2025 SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (SICE ISCS)
abstract: The increase in space debris threatens satellite orbits and raises collision risks. Active Debris Removal (ADR) missions, particularly those targeting large debris in congested orbits, are essential to mitigate the danger. This paper considers low-cost ADR missions using a small satellite to deorbit large debris. Continuous control is employed in a few phases of non-cooperative rendezvous for efficient operations, though stability issues may arise with conventional PD controllers. Additionally, accurate differential drag estimation is needed to keep to an operational timeline and minimize fuel use, but various uncertainties in the orbital environment complicate this issue. We present a trajectory controller based on an onboard differential drag observer, validated via simulation to ensure stable, efficient non-cooperation rendezvous.

articleTitle: Design and Development of A Dual-Band Wide Bandwidth Antenna with Beam Switching for 5G Wireless Communications
publicationTitle: 2025 SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (SICE ISCS)
abstract: This paper presents the design of a 5G switched-beam dual-band antenna capable of operating at 0.7 GHz and 2.6 GHz, addressing the growing demands of modern wireless communication systems. The proposed antenna features grooves and parasitic elements to enhance bandwidth performance, a critical parameter for efficient signal transmission and reception. Additionally, the antenna employs a short-circuiting mechanism to enable main beam switching in two distinct directions, a functionality that aligns with adaptive and intelligent control principles. The measured bandwidth of the antenna is 15.35 MHz at 0.7 GHz and 72.83 MHz at 2.6 GHz, with bandwidth improvements of 5.22 MHz at 0.7 GHz and 8.66 MHz at 2.6 GHz compared to a conventional antenna. These improvements represent a 51.53% increase at 0.7 GHz and a 13.5% increase at 2.6 GHz, showcasing significant performance enhancements. The lightweight, compact, and simple structure of the antenna makes it suitable for practical applications in 5G networks. The design process involved the application of computational methods and modeling techniques using specialized simulation software to optimize the antenna's parameters for beam switching and bandwidth improvement. This work bridges advanced antenna design and control applications, contributing to the development of efficient and reliable communication systems.

articleTitle: Predictive Vehicle Control at Intersections with Look-Ahead Driving Approach
publicationTitle: 2025 SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (SICE ISCS)
abstract: This paper presents a look-ahead vehicle control scheme for efficient traffic management at signalized inter-sections. The proposed scheme predicts future driving states with a look-ahead approach as an extended adaptive cruise control (ACC) model. It maintains car-following behavior similar to human driving while predicting future states of traffic flow to minimize intersection clearing time and aggressive braking independently, similar to model predictive control (MPC) approaches. In contrast to MPC models that are computationally demanding and have limited practical applications due to real-time constraints, the proposed scheme uses a modified Intelligent Driver Model (IDM) with predictive adjustments. The efficiency of the control scheme is evaluated through simulations with multiple vehicles in intersection traffic scenarios, focusing on maintaining safe time headway within a traffic flow and ensuring efficient flows with higher intersection throughput. Comparative results indicate improvements in intersection clearance, human-like vehicle headway management, and enhanced traffic flow performance.

articleTitle: An Analysis of Visual Modeling without Geometric Features for Non-Planar Sloshing
publicationTitle: 2025 SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (SICE ISCS)
abstract: This paper partially proposes an analysis method for evaluating a basis in terms of a linearization error when modeling non-planar sloshing, in visual feedback without geometric features. In the context of the visual feedback, despite the importance, no analysis methods are reported in terms of the linearization error. The proposed analysis method consists of a set of the two terms related to the linearization error. The validity of the proposed method is confirmed experimentally.

articleTitle: Minimum-Order Exosystem-Model-Based Disturbance Observer
publicationTitle: 2025 SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (SICE ISCS)
abstract: This paper considers a minimum-order observer for the augmented system consisting of the nominal plant model and disturbance generating model (exosystem model). This paper shows that this minimum-order exosystem-model-based observer acts as a disturbance observer. Shikada and Sebe showed that the inverse-model-based disturbance observer can be realized as a full-order Luenberger-type observer for the nominal model. On the other hand, the exosystem-model-based disturbance observer is a full-order observer for the augmented system consisting of the nominal plant model and the exosystem model. Accordingly, the order of the exosystem-model-based disturbance observer is higher than that of the inverse-model-based disturbance observer. The minimum-order exosystem-model-based disturbance observer considered in this paper fills the gap of the difference in order. Furthermore, this paper also clarifies the one-to-one correspondence to the Luenberger-type disturbance observer for the nominal plant model. This correspondence shows that the minimum-order exosystem-model-based disturbance observer can achieve the same characteristics as the inverse-model-based disturbance observer.

articleTitle: Precise Estimation Based on Particle Filter for Angular Velocity of Brushless DC Motors with Low Resolution Hall Sensors
publicationTitle: 2025 SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (SICE ISCS)
abstract: Hall sensors are used to estimate angular velocities of brushless DC motors based on the signals. However, the estimation performance deteriorates when the motors operate at low speed due to the low resolution of Hall sensors. To address this problem, this paper proposes a method to improve the estimation performance considering the low resolution of Hall sensors. When the Hall sensor signal is not obtained during low-speed rotation, the proposed method, interprets this situation as the amount of motor rotation being lower the resolution; this information is used for estimation. The estimation algorithm is constructed based on a particle filter. Numerical simulation is used to verify the effectiveness of the proposed method.

articleTitle: Robust Positivizing and Stabilizing Controllers for Prescribed Positive Equilibria
publicationTitle: 2025 SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (SICE ISCS)
abstract: Parameters and set pints of external variables in differential equations influence not only equilibria and their stability, but also system positivity. It sharply contrasts with the artificial but standard control formulation in which zero of the state is always an equilibrium, and we concentrate on the stability of the zero equilibrium. This paper deals with non-zero equilibria of nonlinear dynamics variables whose realizable domains are positive, such as mass, concentration, population, and logistic quantities. Once a desired positive point is picked in the state space, we first need to determine set points of input variables to render the point an equilibrium, Then, we design a feedback control to ensure the state variables their positivity and convergence to the equilibrium. Moreover, we want to have the control mechanism equipped with robustness for uncertainties and disturbances. This paper proposes a novel approach to this problem by using positivizing Lyapunov functions formulated with asymmetric supply rates.

articleTitle: Adaptive Controller Tuning by Factorized VRFT and Recursive Least-Squares
publicationTitle: 2025 SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (SICE ISCS)
abstract: This paper focuses on Factorized VRFT (F-VRFT) which is one of the data-driven control methods and proposes a new adaptive controller tuning method that takes advantage of F-VRFT. In particular, we focus on the fact that the cost function of F-VRFT is quadratic, and thus adaptive optimization is available. In this paper, we propose an adaptive controller tuning method that combines F-VRFT and the Recursive Least-Squares (RLS) algorithm. The effectiveness of the proposed method is verified through numerical examples.

articleTitle: Time-Discretized Simulation Approach for Safety Analysis of Vehicle Platoons Under Sudden Braking and Communication Losses
publicationTitle: 2025 SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (SICE ISCS)
abstract: Vehicle platoons are known to improve traffic efficiency by utilizing coordinated control laws and wireless communication between vehicles. In this paper, we investigate the safety of vehicle platoons. In particular, we explore how the inter-vehicular distances in a vehicle platoon change under sudden braking and drastic levels of communication losses. We use a simulation-based approach to calculate the minimum of all minimum inter-vehicular distances across time for a given set of control parameters that guarantee string stability. For our discrete-time simulations, we propose a method to choose the length of intervals between time-discretization points to guarantee that errors in inter-vehicle distance approximations are bounded by a specific value at all times. Through a numerical example, we show that among control parameters that guarantee string stability some perform better for safety.

articleTitle: Enhancing State Estimator Performance in Networked Control Systems with Sequential Packet Drops via Adaptive Power Control and Error Correction Coding: An Experimental Evaluation
publicationTitle: 2025 SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (SICE ISCS)
abstract: Networked control systems mark a significant advancement in modern control technology, enabling control loops to be closed via communication networks. These systems are designed to be modular and scalable by distributing various functional blocks across different physical locations, interconnected through wireless channels. A major limitation of such systems lies in the inherent imperfection of wireless channels, which can significantly degrade system performance. These effects can be intensified by impairments like fading, which introduce time-varying attenuation and phase shifts, leading to delays and sequential packet losses. To address the issue of sequential data drops, an adaptive power control strategy was investigated to significantly reduce sequential packet drops, complemented by an error correction coding scheme to minimize the error rate. A modified state estimation algorithm has been developed, with its effectiveness validated through numerical simulations and further supported by experimental evaluation using a dedicated testbed built with software-defined radio systems.

articleTitle: A Reduction Approach to Incentive Stackelberg Games for Stochastic Mean-Field Social Control
publicationTitle: 2025 SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (SICE ISCS)
abstract: This paper addresses an incentive Stackelberg game for mean-field stochastic systems. It is found that when the number of followers, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N$</tex>, is infinite, the costs associated with mean field incentives are not well defined, leading to infinite control efforts. To resolve this problem, we introduce new scaling parameters for the system coefficients, inspired by the perturbation approach, and establish reduced-order incentive strategies that ensure a finite cost for the follower incentives. This parameter-independent strategy allows for finite energy costs and enables to reduce the computation of strategies. Our results demonstrate that the proposed incentive strategy achieves near-optimality by transforming the fullorder incentive game problem into a low-dimensional algebraic problem. This approach reveals asymptotic properties of social costs by leveraging the limit of the small parameter ε = 1/ (N + 1). Consequently, instead of requiring large dimensions of R(N+1)n×(N+1)n to compute a centralized strategy, it can be computed within the dimensions R<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">n×n</sup> for each follower, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n$</tex> represents the follower's system dimension, resulting in a significant reduction in computational effort.

articleTitle: An Incentive-based Parking Management System for Reducing Congestion During Peak Demands
publicationTitle: 2025 SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (SICE ISCS)
abstract: Optimal allocation of cars remains a challenge in intelligent parking management systems, particularly during high-demand periods when a parking lot is almost fully occupied. This paper introduces an incentive-based parking management system that influences incoming car patterns using incentives to alleviate parking congestion during peak demand periods. Specifically, we analyze the incoming car patterns at a shopping complex parking facility in Japan, identifying the periods of high congestion or peak activity, which are then used to develop an incentive model. By offering incentives, users with flexible behavior are encouraged to adjust their parking schedule from high-demand periods to those with low-demand periods. The proposed incentive-based management system successfully reduces peak occupancy levels, ultimately preventing congestion from the parking system.

articleTitle: Parameter Identification and Validation of a PMSG Model with Multi-Buck Converter Control Strategy and MPPT Integration
publicationTitle: 2025 SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (SICE ISCS)
abstract: This study presents a comprehensive approach for parameter acquisition and modeling of a Permanent Magnet Synchronous Generator (PMSG) in a wind turbine application. Various connections and measurements were performed to obtain accurate electrical parameters, followed by verification through open-circuit tests to validate the data. A data-driven model of the PMSG was developed in MATLAB/Simulink, with simulated outputs compared to real system measurements for validation. To achieve optimal energy conversion, a control strategy using a multi-phase converter was proposed. Specifically, a parallel configuration of four buck converters was implemented to distribute the current. A Perturb and Observe (P&O) Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) algorithm was applied to adjust the duty cycle which is synchronized across all converters. The results demonstrate that the proposed system and control strategy effectively manage the PMSG power output at simulation level, with the model achieving close alignment to real system performance.

articleTitle: Nonlinear Optimal Control of Electron Dynamics Within Hartree-Fock Theory
publicationTitle: 2025 SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (SICE ISCS)
abstract: Consider the problem of determining the optimal applied electric field to drive a molecule from an initial state to a desired target state. For even moderately sized molecules, solving this problem directly using the exact equations of motion—the time-dependent Schrödinger equation (TDSE)—is numerically intractable. We present a solution of this problem within time-dependent Hartree-Fock (TDHF) theory, a mean field approximation of the TDSE. Optimality is defined in terms of minimizing the total control effort while maximizing the overlap between desired and achieved target states. We frame this problem as an optimization problem constrained by the nonlinear TDHF equations; we solve it using trust region optimization with gradients computed via a custom-built adjoint state method. For three molecular systems, we show that with very small neural network parametrizations of the control, our method yields solutions that achieve desired targets within acceptable constraints and tolerances.

articleTitle: Closed-Loop Safety of Autonomous Vehicles During Lane-Changing with RCI-Tubes
publicationTitle: 2025 SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (SICE ISCS)
abstract: In traditional vehicle lane-changing trajectory planning, an open-loop trajectory is first generated using a nominal model, followed by a closed-loop controller to track this trajectory. However, due to uncertainties, it is challenging to predict the transient error of the closed-loop trajectory over a finite horizon within this framework, and the trajectory that is safe in the open-loop may not necessarily remain safe in the closed-loop. To address this, we propose a planning approach using finite horizon robust control invariant (RCI) tubes. This method involves deriving RCI tubes in advance, ensuring that the entire RCI tube trajectory remains collision-free during planning, thereby guaranteeing closed-loop safety for the lane-changing control system. Additionally, we compare this approach with the currently popular control barrier function (CBF)-based method. Theoretical analysis and simulation results indicate that our approach more clearly captures the propagation of uncertainty in the closed-loop system, whereas the CBF-based method provides a safety margin that is challenging to define in advance, often leading to more conservative behavior. Our method ensures both the flexibility of the lane-changing process and closed-loop safety, avoiding excessive conservatism.

articleTitle: Overview of SICE ISCS 2025
publicationTitle: 2025 SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (SICE ISCS)
abstract: The SICE International Symposium on Control Systems (ISCS) is an event launched in 2015 by the Control Division of the Society of Instrument and Control Engineers (SICE). The ISCS provides an opportunity of international interactions among researchers, students, and engineers who are working on various aspects of control systems, from theory to application.
